title.en: Ren Shi, the Fox-Woman Who Wanted an Ordinary Marriage

region.en: Chang'an, the west market and the hunting parks (Tang capital)

texts.period: Taiping Guangji, juan 452, from Shen Jiji's chuanqi 'Renshi Zhuan' (Tang, c. 780 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 452: Ren Shi the fox-woman, Zheng Liu's marriage, and the hounds of the hunting field

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Zheng Liu met the loveliest woman of Chang'an by the west market — a fox, his companion's hound told them, and she fled with the fox's speed of nine turns. But she came back, and married Zheng: she fed his poor household from stores no one could trace, turned down a great man's lust with the fox's wit, and died at last on the road south — not by hound but by chance — where she had once said, laughing, that foxes have no luck but what they make.
summary.zh: 任氏為狐，遇鄭六於長安西市；犬逐之，任氏遁而復返，與鄭六同居；富家供給、拒豪家之暴；後隨鄭南行，卒於道——『異類之有情者』。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Zheng Liu met her by the west market, the loveliest woman in Chang'an; his friend's hound broke loose and ran at her, and she fled with a fox's nine turns of speed — a fox, then. But she came back to Zheng by her own road, and asked of him no fortune: only a house, a table, and the name of wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 452, Renshi Zhuan (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: She furnished his poverty from stores no ledger could trace, fed his friends, and when a great man of the city took her by force, she broke his grip with words alone — shamed him, reasoned him, and walked free while he stood red-faced in his own hall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 452; not verbatim.

passages.text: She died on the south road, not by hound but by chance, as the foxes' luck ran; and the storyteller's point outlasts the plot: of all the strange women in the tales, the fox was the most faithful — the supernatural judged not by its shape but by its keeping of an ordinary promise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 452, the ending; not verbatim.

title.en: Nie Yinniang, the Nun's Assassin and the Magistrate's Daughter

region.en: The Wei-bo camp and the stone caves of the mountains (Tang frontier)

texts.period: Taiping Guangji, juan 194, from the 'Nie Yinniang' chuanqi (Tang, c. 820 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 194: the stolen daughter, the five years of knife-training, and the two assassins who married

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: A nun took the five-year-old daughter of the Wei-bo garrison commander from her garden and returned her five years later as a knife that killed in the dark without a sound; the commander set her on his rivals. She married a mirror-polisher, defected to a worthier lord with one warning gift, and ended the tale as a chemical hermit — swallowed a drug, grew like a clam-shell, and told her husband to to wait: twenty years, then a crane called at the grave. The first great assassin of Chinese fiction, and its first story of a woman choosing her own lord.
summary.zh: 尼竊魏博大將之女隱娘，五年歸，能於暗中刺人；許嫁磨鏡少年；棄魏帥而事劉昌裔；終以藥化形，不知所之——唐傳奇第一刺客。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: The nun came to the garrison commander's garden, lifted his five-year-old girl out of play, and was gone; five years later she returned the child grown silent and sure — a knife trained in the dark caves to take lives without a sound, as practice on men the nun called the wicked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, Nie Yinniang entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The father set her on his enemies, and she served — until she met the one lord worth serving, warned him by a mirror-gift left at his gate, and went over to his camp against her father's own paymaster; her husband, a mere mirror-polisher, was kept on as her assistant: the tale's quiet joke about marriages arranged by nuns.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, the defection; not verbatim.

passages.text: She ended as the tale's strangest image: a drug that made her body close like a clam, a husband told to wait twenty years by a grave, and a crane that called at last from the cloud-line where she had gone. The knife became a hermit; the daughter of a warlord walked out of her father's war entirely.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, the clam-shell ending; not verbatim.

title.en: The Kunlun Slave and the Locked Tower of the Cui Mansion

region.en: Chang'an, the Cui mansion and the locked red tower (Tang capital)

texts.period: Taiping Guangji, juan 194, from the 'Kunlun Nu' chuanqi (Tang, c. 830 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 194: the slave Mole, the walls of the great house, and the fifty dogs of the garden

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The young scholar Cui fell for a singing-girl kept in a locked tower of the great marshal's compound; his house-servant Mole, a man of Kunlun with iron wrists, carried him over the walls at night, dropped the guard dogs with thrown stones, brought the girl down with the scholar, and did it twice more before the marshal's men came with halberds. Mole fought them off, walked out of the compound, and vanished: the first great emancipator-hero of Chinese fiction, a slave who freed three people and himself with the same pair of wrists.
summary.zh: 崑崙奴磨勒負崔生逾牆入紅綃女宅，遣猛犬，竊紅綃與崔生俱出；軍士圍捕，磨勒脫身而去——異域之力士。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text. The Kunlun figure reflects Tang-era African/Indian Ocean servitude — the tale's exoticizing frame is noted critically.

passages.text: Cui the young scholar loved a singing-girl kept in a locked tower of the great marshal's household; his servant Mole, a man of Kunlun with wrists of iron, said only: show me the wall — and carried the scholar over it at midnight, past the dogs of the garden, into the tower's chamber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, Kunlun Nu entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The girl asked to be carried out of her gilded prison with him; Mole took her down the wall on his back and walked her home through the sleeping city, and did the same errand twice more before the marshal's men finally traced the escapes and came with halberds to the servants' quarters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194; not verbatim.

passages.text: Mole scattered the halberdiers with his two hands, stepped over the compound wall unhurried, and was never seen in the city again — a slave who freed a scholar, a girl, and himself with the same skill, and paid for it with nothing but his own disappearance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 194, the ending; not verbatim.

title.en: Hongxian, the Red Thread Across a Governor's Pillow

region.en: The camps of Luzhou and Weibo (Tang frontier, Hebei–Shanxi)

texts.period: Taiping Guangji, juan 195, from the 'Hongxian' chuanqi (Tang, c. 830 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 195: the maidservant who flew three hundred li, took a gold box, and stopped a war with it

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The governor of Luzhou's household held a maidservant, Hongxian, who could fly three hundred li in a night with a red thread tied to her brow. When the warlord of Weibo massed an army to destroy the governor, she rode the night wind into his bedroom, stood at his sleeping head with her knife — and took, instead of his life, the gold box at his pillow, flying home by dawn. The box laid on the warlord's own breakfast-table stopped the war; the maidservant was, she said, a man of an earlier age reborn to pay a debt of one city's blood.
summary.zh: 紅線夜入魏博節度使田承嗣寢帳，取其枕前金盒而歸；承嗣懼而罷兵——紅線自言前生為男子，以誤傷人命，謫為女子償之。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: When the warlord of Weibo massed his armies to destroy the governor of Luzhou, the governor's own maidservant Hongxian asked for one night and a red thread tied at her brow; she flew the three hundred li to the warlord's camp in the dark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 195, Hongxian entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: In his bedroom she stood over the sleeping man with her knife at his head, and considered — the war to be paid in one life, or taught in one theft. She took the gold box from his pillow, left the knife, and flew home before dawn with the proof of how far a servant can reach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 195, the theft; not verbatim.

passages.text: The box was laid on the warlord's own breakfast-table by his own envoy, with a courteous letter; the warlord, understanding in one look that his bedroom had been visited by the household he meant to destroy, recalled his armies. The maidservant said farewell to her master and vanished — a man of an earlier age, she said, reborn as a woman to pay an old debt, and paid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 195, the ending; not verbatim.

title.en: Laozi Born Old, and the Ox Through the Western Pass

region.en: The Hangu Pass, west of Luoyang (Shaanxi–Henan)

texts.period: Shenxian Zhuan (Biographies of Divine Immortals) by Ge Hong, c. 300 CE, Laozi biography

source.work: Shenxian Zhuan, 'Laozi': the ancient mother's plum-? — the ancient origin, the keeper Yin Xi's request, and the five thousand characters

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The immortal biographies make Laozi the oldest of beings, born as an old man with white hair, and a keeper of archives in the declining Zhou. When the age decayed he rode a black ox toward the western passes; the gate-keeper Yin Xi saw the purple vapor riding the east wind and held the gate until the sage wrote down, in five thousand characters, the Way and its Power — then rode on west, leaving behind the smallest book and the largest theology.
summary.zh: 老子生而皓首，故稱老子；周室衰，乘青牛西出關；關令尹喜見紫氣東來，留之——為著五千言《道德經》，遂西去莫知所終。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shenxian Zhuan biography; the historical Laozi of the Shiji is a different genre — both are kept apart in the corpus.

passages.text: The immortal record says Laozi was older than heaven and earth, and was born with white hair — hence his name, the Old Child — and served the declining house of Zhou as keeper of the archives, watching the world's receipts pile up without its wisdom growing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, Laozi biography (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the dynasty could no longer be helped, he mounted a black ox and rode west toward the passes. The gate-keeper Yin Xi, a student of the skies, saw a purple vapor riding the east wind and knew a sage was coming: he held the gate and asked for the teaching as toll.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, Yin Xi episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: Laozi stayed the night and wrote, in five thousand characters, the book of the Way and its Power; then he rode on through the pass and west beyond all records — the smallest book and the largest theology left at a customs gate, and the sage gone where no account of him follows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, the departure; not verbatim.

title.en: The Yellow Emperor Casts the Tripod and Rides the Dragon From Dinghu

region.en: Mount Jing and the tripod-pool of Dinghu (Shaanxi)

texts.period: Shenxian Zhuan by Ge Hong, c. 300 CE, Huangdi biography; parallel in Shiji, Fengshan Shu

source.work: Shenxian Zhuan, 'Huangdi': the first tripod cast at Mount Jing, the dragon that came down, and the ministers clinging to the whiskers

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Having united the world, the Yellow Emperor mined the copper of Mount Jing and cast a tripod at the pool called Dinghu; when it was done a dragon came down with its whiskers hanging, and the emperor, his household and seventy ministers climbed aboard and rose. Those who could not climb seized the dragon's whiskers, which tore out and fell with the bows the crowd had clutched — and the village keeps the names to this day: Whisker Row, Bow-Grasping Hamlet, and the pool named Tripod-Lake.
summary.zh: 黃帝採首山銅，鑄鼎於荊山下；鼎既成，有龍垂胡髯下迎黃帝；黃帝上騎，群臣後宮從上者七十餘人；小臣不得上，持龍髯，髯拔墮，弓亦墮地；百姓抱弓而號，其弓曰烏號，其地曰鼎湖。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Shenxian Zhuan biography and the Shiji parallel.

passages.text: The Yellow Emperor, having set the world in order, mined the copper of the first mountain and cast a great tripod at the pool of Dinghu — the cauldron of the state's completion, cast in the one metal worth the sky's attention.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, Huangdi biography (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tripod finished, a dragon came down with its whiskers trailing, and the emperor with his family and seventy of his ministers climbed upon it and rose from the pool into the clouds; the crowd below seized the whiskers and the bows of the departing — and the whiskers tore out and fell, and with them the bows. The villages of that mountain keep the names the fall earned: Whisker Row where the beard landed, Bow-Grasping Hamlet where the crowd held on, and the pool named Tripod-Lake — the founding emperor's exit from history filed as geography.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan, the ascension; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Shenxian Zhuan with the Shiji parallel; not verbatim.

title.en: The Queen Mother of the West Feasts Emperor Wu, and the Peach Thieves Come

region.en: The palace of Emperor Wu at Chang'an (Han court)

texts.period: Han Wudi Neizhuan (Inner Biography of Emperor Wu), c. 4th-5th c. CE; parallel in Han Wudi Zhuan

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; the text via digitized collections)
source.work: Han Wudi Neizhuan: Xiwangmu's descent on the azure bird, the seven peaches of three-thousand-year ripening, and Dongfang Shuo caught at the window

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: On the seventh month's seventh day the Queen Mother of the West came down to Emperor Wu's palace on a chariot of purple clouds drawn by azure birds; she brought with her attendants and, wrapped in leaves, seven peaches of the garden where one ripening takes three thousand years. She gave two to the Emperor; the third vanished from the tray — and the Queen Mother laughed, for she knew who had taken it: Dongfang Shuo, her own thieving courtier, caught at the window with the peach in his mouth.
summary.zh: 漢武帝好仙道，西王母以七月七日降於宮中，命侍女索桃；桃盤盛七枚，大如鴨卵；王母以四枚與帝，自食其三，帝收其核欲種之——東方朔窺桃竊之，王母笑指之：『此桃三千年一生實。』

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Neizhuan text.

passages.text: The Emperor Wu of Han, hungry for the Way of the immortals, purified a palace tower, and on the night of the seventh month the Queen Mother of the West descended on a cloud-chariot of purple vapor, drawn by the azure birds that serve her and attended by a train of her singing-women.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Han Wudi Neizhuan (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: She called for peaches, and a plate was brought from heaven's orchard: seven peaches of a size like a duck's egg, from the tree that ripens once in three thousand years. She gave two to the emperor, who ate and wanted the kernels to plant — and she laughed at the wish, for the tree of that garden does not grow in soil such as his.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Han Wudi Neizhuan, the peaches; not verbatim.

passages.text: A third peach vanished from the plate while she spoke; the Queen Mother looked at the window and said, still laughing, the thief's name: Dongfang Shuo, her courtier, was already swallowing it behind the lattice — the peach-thief of heaven's garden employed, for the joke of it, in the emperor's own council hall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Han Wudi Neizhuan, Dongfang Shuo episode; not verbatim.

title.en: Du Zichun, the Man Who Could Not Stay Silent in Hell

region.en: The tower of the ascetics on Mount Song (Henan)

texts.period: Taiping Guangji, juan 16, from the 'Du Zichun' tale (Tang, c. 750 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 16: the squanderer made rich twice, the vow of silence, and the hell of every passion

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Du Zichun, a squanderer made rich twice by a strange old man, was given one trial for the third gift: keep silent in a tower for a day, whatever comes. All day hell came to him — lightning, demons, boiling cauldrons, the general's blade at his neck, his wife's head dropped in the fire, rebirth as a girl mute and scorned, marriage, a son — and his child, dashed against a stone, laughed in his face. At that his tongue unlocked with one cry of grief — and the tower's fire went out: the elixir needed a heart with no passions left, and his had one.
summary.zh: 杜子春兩受老人贈金；第三試：嵩山煉丹爐前終日緘口；歷雷電、刀山、油鼎、畜生道，為啞女生子；兒撲石而笑，子春失聲而呼——爐火遂熄，丹不成。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Du Zichun had squandered one fortune and been given a second by a strange old man in the market; squandered that too, and been given a third with a condition: a day's vigil of total silence in the old man's mountain tower, whatever came for him there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 16, Du Zichun entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The day brought hell in order: a storm that split the tower, generals and demons who beat and boiled and burned him, his wife's head dropped screaming into the fire — and he held. Then he was reborn in the vision as a mute girl, sold, married, given a son; and the son, at her silent mother's knee, laughed and stumbled toward the well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 16, the trials; not verbatim.

passages.text: The child was dashed on the stones and laughed up at her, and Du Zichun's silence broke with one cry of love. The old man's voice came through the smoke: the elixir was ready but the heart was not — for the Way of the immortals wants no passions, and his had one, and it had cost them the furnace. He went home rich for the last time, having failed magnificently.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 16, the failure; not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Man Under the Moon and the Red Thread Ledger

region.en: The temple garden near Song city (Henan)

texts.period: Taiping Guangji, juan 159, from the 'Dinghun Dian' tale (Tang, c. 810 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 159: the moonlit ledger of marriages and the red thread that cannot be broken

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Wei Gu, walking in the moonlight at a temple near Song, found an old man reading a ledger against a bag of red threads; the ledger, the man said, was the book of all marriages, and one thread tied ankle to ankle joined two people wherever they ran. Wei Gu laughed at the entry that assigned him a greengrocer's baby daughter — and the old man, to settle it, took him by night to the vegetable market, where a woman with a scarred child of the vegetable stall sat selling greens. Wei Gu sent a servant to stab the child; she survived the knife with a scar over the brow. Years on, the magistrate gave him a daughter of beauty and brow-scarred: the greengrocer's baby, led by the red thread he had tried to cut.
summary.zh: 韋固遇月下老人於宋城，赤繩繫足以定婚姻；固怒遣僕刺菜市女孩，十四年後娶妻眉間有刀痕——月老祠由此立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text. The child-stabbing episode is recorded as the tale's darker layer.

passages.text: Wei Gu walked in the moonlight outside a temple near Song and found an old man on the steps reading a ledger, with a bag of red threads at his feet; the ledger, the man said, was the book of all marriages, and a single red thread, tied ankle to ankle, joined every pair it named — however far they ran to escape it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 159, Dinghun Dian entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: He showed Wei Gu his own entry: a daughter of the vegetable market, a baby in a cradle by the greens. Wei Gu, insulted, sent a servant that night to stab the child; the knife left a scar over the brow and the child lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 159, the stabbing; not verbatim.

passages.text: Fourteen years on, the magistrate gave Wei Gu his daughter in marriage — a beauty, and brow-scarred; she told him at her mirror how she had been a grocer's baby stabbed in the cradle and adopted by an uncle. Wei Gu told her about the old man with the threads; both believed, and the temple of the Old Man Under the Moon has stood in the tale's honor ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 159, the marriage; not verbatim.

title.en: Pei Hang and the Blue-Bridge of the Jade Mortar

region.en: The Blue-Bridge post-station on the Shang mountain road (Shaanxi)

texts.period: Taiping Guangji, juan 50, from Pei Xing's 'Pei Hang' tale (Tang, c. 860 CE)

source.work: Taiping Guangji, juan 50: the jade pestle and the hundred days of pounding herbs at the Blue Bridge

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Pei Hang, riding home in splendor, stopped at the Blue-Bridge station for water and heard the girl behind the curtain sing his own verse back at him — Yunying, the hostess's daughter, a girl of heaven's stock. An old woman demanded his jewels for the marriage; a master of the mountains told him the true price: a jade pestle, and a hundred days of pounding the herb of the immortals in the inn's own courtyard. He bought the pestle, pounded for a hundred days in the drizzle, and married Yunying — and the two were seen later riding a jade-lion into the clouds, inviters of the household of the immortals.
summary.zh: 裴航藍橋驛遇雲英；老嫗索玉杵臼為聘，航傾財購之，搗藥百日而娶雲英——夫婦俱仙去。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Taiping Guangji text.

passages.text: Pei Hang, richly dressed and riding home from a failed examination, stopped at the Blue-Bridge station for water; behind the partition a girl's voice sang three lines that matched his own heart's verse — Yunying, the innkeeper's daughter, who was not of the innkeeper's stock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 50, Pei Hang entry (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old hostess named a bride-price no man could pay: a jade pestle and mortar of the immortals, and a hundred days of pounding the herb that opens the Way. Pei Hang sold his estates, hunted the jade through the markets of the capital, found it, and came back to the Blue Bridge to work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 50; not verbatim.

passages.text: A hundred days he pounded in the courtyard, hands in the drizzle, herbs to powder, powder to medicine; on the last night the doors of the inn opened on a hill of light, and the household came up the mountain as immortal guests. Years after, travelers saw two riders on a jade lion in the clouds and knew the pairing at the Blue Bridge had ended in heaven's register.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taiping Guangji, juan 50, the ascent; not verbatim.
